data.sourcePassage:
Technology is often presented as a clean, invisible alternative to physical products, but computing has a substantial environmental footprint at every stage of its lifecycle.

Data centres — vast warehouses of servers that power cloud storage, streaming services, and websites — collectively consume approximately one to two percent of the world's electricity. They run continuously, generating heat that requires enormous cooling systems, which themselves use large amounts of electricity and water. When this electricity is generated from fossil fuels, significant quantities of CO₂ are released into the atmosphere.

Before a device is ever switched on, its manufacture has already caused environmental damage. Producing a single smartphone generates around 70 kg of CO₂ equivalent. Manufacturing requires mining rare earth minerals such as cobalt and lithium, high-temperature smelting, precision assembly in clean-room facilities, and global shipping — all energy-intensive processes that often damage local ecosystems.

When devices reach the end of their lives, they become e-waste. Over 50 million tonnes of electronic waste are generated globally each year, yet less than 20% is formally recycled through certified channels. Electronics contain toxic materials — lead, mercury, cadmium, and arsenic — which leach into soil and groundwater when dumped in landfill. Much e-waste is exported to developing countries, where workers, sometimes including children, dismantle it informally in hazardous conditions. Technology companies and governments are under increasing pressure to design products for longevity and repairability rather than planned obsolescence.

data.sourceTitle: Technology and Employment: Automation and the Changing Workforce
data.targetTitle: Technology and Employment: Automation and the Changing Workforce
data.sourcePassage:
Technology has transformed employment throughout history, and the pace of change is accelerating. Automation — the use of machines and software to perform tasks previously done by humans — is reshaping the economy in profound ways, eliminating some roles while creating entirely new ones.

In manufacturing, robots now perform precision assembly, welding, and painting tasks that once employed large numbers of workers. In retail, self-service checkouts have reduced the need for cashiers. In finance, algorithmic trading and automated accounting software process transactions faster and more accurately than human clerks. In transport, driverless vehicles and delivery drones are beginning to displace drivers and couriers. These changes improve productivity and reduce costs for businesses, but can leave workers without income and communities without purpose if jobs disappear faster than new ones emerge.

However, technology also creates new jobs. Demand for software engineers, data scientists, cybersecurity specialists, AI trainers, and digital content creators has grown rapidly. Roles in maintaining, installing, and upgrading technology infrastructure provide employment where none existed before. Many of the jobs that will exist in 20 years have not yet been invented.

The critical challenge is the skills gap. Workers whose jobs are automated often do not have the skills needed for the new roles that technology creates. Retraining programmes, digital literacy education in schools, and investment in lifelong learning are widely recognised as essential responses. The goal is an economy where the benefits of automation are shared broadly, rather than concentrated among those who own the technology.

data.sourceTitle: The Digital Divide and Social Equality
data.targetTitle: The Digital Divide and Social Equality
data.sourcePassage:
The digital divide refers to the gap between those who have reliable access to technology and the internet and those who do not. This divide is not only a matter of owning a device — it also encompasses the skills to use technology effectively, the confidence to engage with digital services, and the speed and reliability of the internet connection available.

In the United Kingdom, the digital divide affects several distinct groups. Elderly people are less likely to have grown up with technology, may lack digital skills and confidence, and can face physical barriers such as poor eyesight or reduced dexterity that make devices difficult to use. Low-income households may be unable to afford a broadband subscription or a suitable device. People in rural areas often have significantly slower or entirely absent internet connections. People with certain disabilities may need assistive technology that is costly or hard to access.

The consequences are serious. Many essential services have moved predominantly online: booking GP appointments, applying for Universal Credit, accessing banking, and searching for jobs. Those excluded from the digital world are therefore excluded from full participation in society. During the COVID-19 pandemic, when schools closed and lessons moved online, the digital divide became starkly visible — students without computers or broadband at home attended no lessons for months.

Addressing the divide requires coordinated action: subsidised devices and broadband for low-income households, free digital skills training in libraries and community centres, and the legal requirement that critical public services remain accessible by non-digital means for those who cannot use them online.
